input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-261: Analysis of Algorithms. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course provides an introduction to the design and analysis of algorithms. It covers a variety of classical algorithms and data structures and their complexity and will equip students with the intellectual tools to design, analyze, implement, and evaluate their own algorithms. Prerequisites:(CSCI-243 and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)) or (SWEN-262 and MATH-241) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[mit-algorithms]
Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.

[opendsa]
OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.

[rit-csci-261]
This course provides an introduction to the design and analysis of algorithms. It covers a variety of classical algorithms and data structures and their complexity and will equip students with the intellectual tools to design, analyze, implement, and evaluate their own algorithms. Prerequisites:(CSCI-243 and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)) or (SWEN-262 and MATH-241) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds.
beats.example: A sorting algorithm must guarantee that the output array contains all input elements in non-decreasing order.
beats.title: Introduction to Algorithm Analysis
beats.visualDirection: Display a split screen showing a problem statement on the left and a resource usage graph on the right, with arrows linking them to indicate the analytical connection.

beats.claim: Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size.
beats.example: Big-O notation for a nested loop sorting algorithm indicates quadratic time complexity, O(n^2), as input size doubles.
beats.title: Asymptotic Notation Basics
beats.visualDirection: Show a line graph with input size on the x-axis and resource units on the y-axis, highlighting a quadratic curve labeled with O(n^2) notation.

beats.claim: A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination.
beats.example: In a linear search, the invariant states that the target element, if present, must be in the unexamined portion of the array.
beats.title: Loop Invariants for Correctness
beats.visualDirection: Animate an array with a moving boundary line, highlighting the unexamined segment and labeling it with the invariant statement.

beats.claim: Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results.
beats.example: Merge sort divides an array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted subarrays into a single ordered array.
beats.title: Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a recursive tree diagram where each node splits into two children, with merge steps shown at the bottom level.

beats.claim: Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms.
beats.example: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes the time complexity of merge sort, solved via the Master Theorem.
beats.title: Recurrence Relations
beats.visualDirection: Display a mathematical recurrence equation alongside a step-by-step expansion showing how T(n) breaks down into smaller subproblems.

beats.claim: Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms.
beats.example: An adjacency list for a directed graph stores each vertex followed by a list of its outgoing edges, enabling efficient neighbor lookups.
beats.title: Graph Representation
beats.visualDirection: Render a directed graph with nodes and arrows, then overlay an adjacency list table showing each vertex mapped to its connected neighbors.

beats.claim: Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions.
beats.example: Breadth-first search explores all vertices at a given depth before moving to the next level, ensuring the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
beats.title: Graph Traversal Methods
beats.visualDirection: Animate a queue-based traversal where vertices are visited level by level, with distance markers indicating path length from the source.

beats.claim: Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.
beats.example: Choosing a hash table over a linked list for key-value storage reduces lookup time from O(n) to O(1) average case, provided a good collision strategy is used.
beats.title: Data Structure Selection
beats.visualDirection: Compare two side-by-side data structures, highlighting operation costs and invariant constraints for each, with a decision flowchart guiding the choice.

beats.claim: A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.
beats.example: Before coding, a developer specifies the input array and expected sorted output, verifies correctness via trace, and calculates O(n log n) time and O(n) space requirements.
beats.title: Algorithm Design Process
beats.visualDirection: Show a three-step workflow diagram: Input/Output specification -> Correctness proof -> Complexity analysis, with checkmarks indicating completion.

beats.claim: Students must verify that their algorithm design addresses correctness, resource bounds, and representation efficiency before implementation.
beats.example: The checklist confirms that the loop invariant holds, asymptotic bounds are calculated, and graph traversal uses the appropriate adjacency structure for the problem constraints.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a printable checklist template with three columns: Correctness Verification, Resource Analysis, and Representation Efficiency, ready for student annotation.

learningObjectives: Define and apply asymptotic notation to describe the growth rate of algorithmic resource usage relative to input size.
Construct and verify a loop invariant to prove the correctness of iterative algorithms through initialization, maintenance, and termination.
Represent and traverse graph structures using adjacency lists to solve reachability and path-finding problems.

input.text: With the foundation in place, examine how Loop Invariants for Correctness operates in a concrete sequence. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Consider this worked case: In a linear search, the invariant states that the target element, if present, must be in the unexamined portion of the array. On screen, animate an array with a moving boundary line, highlighting the unexamined segment and labeling it with the invariant statement. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.

Begin by framing Introduction to Algorithm Analysis as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Consider this worked case: A sorting algorithm must guarantee that the output array contains all input elements in non-decreasing order. On screen, display a split screen showing a problem statement on the left and a resource usage graph on the right, with arrows linking them to indicate the analytical connection. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.

Apply Recurrence Relations to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Consider this worked case: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes the time complexity of merge sort, solved via the Master Theorem. On screen, display a mathematical recurrence equation alongside a step-by-step expansion showing how T(n) breaks down into smaller subproblems. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.

Use Data Structure Selection to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible. Consider this worked case: Choosing a hash table over a linked list for key-value storage reduces lookup time from O(n) to O(1) average case, provided a good collision strategy is used. On screen, compare two side-by-side data structures, highlighting operation costs and invariant constraints for each, with a decision flowchart guiding the choice. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.

Next, compare the choices involved in Divide-and-Conquer Strategy and make the decision criteria explicit. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Consider this worked case: Merge sort divides an array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted subarrays into a single ordered array. On screen, illustrate a recursive tree diagram where each node splits into two children, with merge steps shown at the bottom level. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.

Stress-test the reasoning around Graph Traversal Methods with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Consider this worked case: Breadth-first search explores all vertices at a given depth before moving to the next level, ensuring the shortest path in unweighted graphs. On screen, animate a queue-based traversal where vertices are visited level by level, with distance markers indicating path length from the source. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.

Examine the tradeoffs in Graph Representation, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Consider this worked case: An adjacency list for a directed graph stores each vertex followed by a list of its outgoing edges, enabling efficient neighbor lookups. On screen, render a directed graph with nodes and arrows, then overlay an adjacency list table showing each vertex mapped to its connected neighbors. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.

Connect Algorithm Design Process to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space. Consider this worked case: Before coding, a developer specifies the input array and expected sorted output, verifies correctness via trace, and calculates O(n log n) time and O(n) space requirements. On screen, show a three-step workflow diagram: Input/Output specification -> Correctness proof -> Complexity analysis, with checkmarks indicating completion. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.

Now define Asymptotic Notation Basics precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. Consider this worked case: Big-O notation for a nested loop sorting algorithm indicates quadratic time complexity, O(n^2), as input size doubles. On screen, show a line graph with input size on the x-axis and resource units on the y-axis, highlighting a quadratic curve labeled with O(n^2) notation. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.

Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. This course provides an introduction to the design and analysis of algorithms. Consider this worked case: The checklist confirms that the loop invariant holds, asymptotic bounds are calculated, and graph traversal uses the appropriate adjacency structure for the problem constraints. On screen, display a printable checklist template with three columns: Correctness Verification, Resource Analysis, and Representation Efficiency, ready for student annotation. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
